theme: The Jerusalem Council; the second journey begins
readingInstruction: Read Acts 15:1-41. Some teach that Gentiles must be circumcised to be saved. The apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem to decide. Notice how they reason, who speaks, and what they conclude. Then Paul and Barnabas part ways.
settingTheScene: This is the central chapter of Acts and arguably the most important meeting in the early church. The question is whether Gentile believers must become Jews, keeping the law of Moses, to be saved. If the answer were yes, the gospel would become another form of Judaism. Around AD 49, the apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem. The decision shapes the whole Christian faith.
observation: “But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (15:1).
“And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us” (15:8).
“Now therefore why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?” (15:10).
“But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will” (15:11).
“After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen” (15:16).
“Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God” (15:19).
“For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements” (15:28).
“And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other” (15:39).
interpretation:
The trouble starts in Antioch when men from Judea teach that circumcision is necessary for salvation. Paul and Barnabas dispute with them, and the church sends them to Jerusalem to settle the matter. There they report how God had opened a door to the Gentiles, but some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees insist that Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses.

After much debate, Peter stands. He reminds them that God chose that Gentiles should hear the gospel from his mouth, and that God, who knows the heart, bore witness by giving the Gentiles the Holy Spirit as he did to the Jews, “having cleansed their hearts by faith.” To impose the law now would be to put God to the test with a yoke that neither they nor their fathers could bear. The conclusion is the heart of the gospel: “We believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.” Jews are saved the same way as Gentiles, by grace, not by law.

Barnabas and Paul describe the signs and wonders God did among the Gentiles. Then James, the brother of Jesus, speaks. He quotes Amos 9:11-12: God will rebuild the fallen tent of David so that the rest of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by his name. The inclusion of the Gentiles is not a departure from the Old Testament but its fulfillment. This is a key text for the progressive covenantalism you have been reading: the Davidic kingdom, restored in Christ, includes the nations. James gives his judgment: do not trouble the Gentiles who turn to God, but write to them to abstain from things polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from what has been strangled, and from blood. These requests promoted fellowship between Jew and Gentile believers, who would share tables. The letter goes out, saying, “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.” The Gentiles rejoice at its encouragement.

Chapter 15 ends with sadness. Paul proposes revisiting the churches, but Barnabas wants to take John Mark again, who had left them on the first journey. Paul refuses. There is a sharp disagreement, and they part. Barnabas takes Mark to Cyprus. Paul chooses Silas and goes through Syria and Cilicia. God uses even this to double the missionary effort. Later Paul writes that Mark is “very useful” to him (2 Timothy 4:11).
connection: Amos 9:11-12 is James’s text. Genesis 17 is the covenant of circumcision. Galatians 2:1-21 is Paul’s account of the same events. Galatians 5:1-6 insists that circumcision no longer matters. Romans 3:28 and 4:1-12 teach justification by faith apart from works of the law. Ephesians 2:8-9 says we are saved by grace through faith. Colossians 2:11-17 shows circumcision and food laws fulfilled in Christ. 2 Timothy 4:11 mentions Mark.
application:
Where are you tempted to add something to grace, such as a rule, a ritual, or a performance?

Rejoice in verse 11 and say it aloud: saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus.

If you’ve had a sharp disagreement with a fellow believer, pray for reconciliation and for God to use it for good.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that you are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus.
Confess where you try to add to grace.
Ask him to help you welcome others without adding burdens.
